judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya & ors v AUNG NAING TUN & ors
judgments.catchwords: Criminal Law — Sentence — Section 304(a) Penal Code — Culpable homicide not amounting to murder — Charge amended from section 302 Penal Code to section 304(a) Penal Code — Plea of guilty — First offender — Mitigating factors — Provocation by deceased — Deceased armed with rubber-tapping knife — Aggravating factors — Sentencing trend — Proportionality — Appropriate sentence — Seven years’ imprisonment from date of arrest. Held; Accused convicted under Section 304(a) of the Penal Code and sentence to seven (7) years’ imprisonment from date of arrest: The Accused was initially charged under section 302 of the Penal Code. The charge was subsequently amended to section 304(a) of the Penal Code, to which the Accused pleaded guilty. In determining the sentence, this Court considered the nature and gravity of the offence, the aggravating factors such as the prevailing sentencing trend and mitigating factors which includes Accused’s plea of guilty and his status as a first offender. This Court also gave substantial weight to the circumstances leading to the offence, including the deceased’s provocation and attack on the Accused with a rubber-tapping knife. Having balanced the competing considerations, the Court imposed seven (7) years’ imprisonment from the date of arrest.

judgments.title: WISEYES SOLUTIONS SDN BHD v Pertubuhan Keselamatan Sosial (PERKESO)
judgments.catchwords: The Plaintiff applied under Order 24 rule 3 of the Rules of Court 2012 for discovery of documents about third-party contractors, chiefly GKSH Sdn Bhd, that the Defendant engaged to work on the ASSIST and EIS systems. The Plaintiff says these contractors, not the Plaintiff, caused the SLA breaches behind the Defendant's RM58.5 million counterclaim. The Court allowed the application, with some limits on scope. Causation was in issue, so the documents were relevant. The Defendant's claim that alteration was technically impossible was a disputed fact in issue at trial. The request was not a fishing expedition because the Defendant admitted engaging GKSH. GKSH held documents within the Defendant's "power." The Defendant must file a verified list of documents and explain on oath any that are no longer in its possession. Costs in the cause. Discovery; Order 24 Rules of Court 2012; relevance and necessity; fishing expedition; possession, custody or power; third-party contractor; SLA counterclaim; causation.

judgments.title: MUHAMMAD HANIFF RAZRI BIN HASRI v Pendakwa Raya & ors
judgments.catchwords: Criminal Justice - Dangerous Drugs Act 1952, ss. 2, 37(d), 39B(1)(a) — Trafficking — Appeal against conviction — Whether statutory presumption of deemed possession under s. 37(d) can be conflated with substantive trafficking under s. 2 by "keeping and storing" without proof of an independent positive overt act beyond reasonable doubt — Presumption stacking and impermissible inversion of burden of proof — Criminal Procedure Code, s. 180(3) — Duty of trial court to amend charge to possession under s. 39A(2) where only s. 37(d) possession proved at close of prosecution case — Mid-trial mutation of case causing incurable prejudice and breach of natural justice — Evidence Act 1950, s. 54(1) — Prejudicial reception of bad character evidence (AADK document and smoking bong) — Break in chain of custody via non-contemporaneous, post-facto reconstruction of Drug Exhibit Register (POL 260) compromising identity of dangerous drugs — Non-exclusive access to ancestral premises and negative forensic nexus — Curative provisions inapplicable where foundational evidence of possession is fatally tainted — Conviction quashed and substituted conviction under s. 39A(2) refused — Accused acquitted and discharged.
